newsitem.title: UK: UK politicians hail digital television revolution.
newsitem.headline: UK politicians hail digital television revolution.

text.p: A digital television revolution is just around the corner and will hold the key to large numbers of jobs, a committee of British politicians said on Tuesday.

A report from parliament's National Heritage Committee also warned restrictions on BBC and British Telecommunications entertainment services could prove to be a serious handicap in the ever-changing world of entertainment broadcasting.
"It is clear that we are on the verge of a revolution," the all-party group of MPs said. "Very large number of jobs are at stake, as well as high sums in trade and exports."
Digital television already has a foothold in much of Europe and in Britain pay television operator BSkyB has said it will launch a 200-channel digital satellite service.

BSkyB will also team up with leading British television companies, Carlton Communications and Granada Group, to apply to run 15 digital terrestrial TV (DTT) channels, including subscription channels from the BBC.
On Monday, the BBC announced it will link up with British satellite cable broadcaster Flextech Plc to offer up to eight new pay television channels.
And all that is just the tip of the iceberg. The Cable Communications Association says digital cable television will offer up to 1,000 channels in the near future.
The National Heritage Committee said digital terrestrial TV may only have a limited future with the long-term way forward in the hands of non-terrestrial digital services.
It appeared to give a tacit thumbs up to the BBC's new venture, saying it saw no reason why sports events should not be shown exclusively on pay-per-view or subscription channels.

But it said the BBC's ability to compete in the broadcasting future was cramped by the fact that its borrowing, which counts as part of Britain's public sector debt, is limited. That restriction should be lifted.
"This concept of restricting borrowing by public sector organisations is outmoded, particularly in the case of the BBC, which is becoming increasingly commercial in orientation."
The MPs also said that technology was now changing so fast that BT will no longer be able to compete unless restrictions placed on the telecoms giant were dropped by the year 2002.

"There is a danger that BT will no longer be able to compete with cable companies. Equally, it is a strange anomaly that the cable companies can offer inducements of telephone services to potential TV companies while BT cannot offer broadcasting services to their telephone customers."
Last month, National Heritage Secretary Virginia Bottomley said the government was right to restrict BT's entertainment services and said the rule would remain in place until 2001.

Turning to Channel 4 -- a state-controlled corporation funded by advertising set up to cater for minority tastes -- the committee said the payments Channel 4 makes to ITV should be ended "as soon as possible."
If Channel 4 revenues exceed 14 percent of the combined advertising and sponsorship income of itself and ITV, it must hand over 50 percent of the surplus to the ITV licensees.

The BBC remains funded by a licence fee levied on anyone who owns a television set and the National Heritage Committee saw no reason to tamper with that now. It still saw the BBC as at the heart of broadcasting, both in Britain and abroad.

"We have the priceless advantage in this country of the unparalleled international recognition of and respect for the BBC," the report said. "The English language is increasingly the most used international language in the world and the BBC is a prime custodian."
